title: What we learned from F1's first visit to the Madring
excerpt:
The addition of a new circuit brings with it adrenaline, curiosity and a sense of trepidation as no one quite knows how its debut will play out – and the Madring certainly delivered on all of the above. Here are the biggest lessons we’ve taken away from the Spanish Grand Prix weekend…

How the drivers tackled a new challenge

There are so many factors that can influence the success of a driver’s race, from unpredictable changes in the weather to split-second strategy calls, but for most of the season, they can at least rely on the consistency of track layouts they’ve learned by heart over the years.

They spend time in the simulator until making a corner comes down to muscle memory, and while they were all able to use the same method of preparation for the Madring, nothing compares to racing around it in real life.

The feel of the freshly laid surface, testing just how close to the walls they could get, taking in the indescribable energy of the Spanish capital… they were only able to experience all of this fully when FP1 began on Friday afternoon.

Home favourite Fernando Alonso called it “very technical” and “attractive”, while some drew comparisons to Jeddah’s high speeds and narrow sections. Like the Saudi Arabian track, the Madring quickly showed its bite, with Arvid Lindblad, Lewis Hamilton and Ollie Bearman all caught out in Free Practice.

Once everyone found the initial limits, they began to push them further and further and the lap times didn’t lie, plummeting by over 2s between FP1 and Lando Norris’ magnificent final effort in Qualifying.

Tyre management was king

It’s well documented that the better a driver can manage the tyres, the more likely they are to do well in a race. Extending a stint opens up greater strategic options, while limiting degradation ensures more grip and, consequently, better stability on track.

Of course, that’s easier said than done, as many discovered at the Madring. George Russell explained after Qualifying that “as the track has got faster, I’ve been struggling to get the most out of the tyres”, which he thought was why he couldn’t fight for pole position and wound up sixth in the session.

Moving onto the the Grand Prix, Nico Hulkenberg scored for just the third time this season as Audi continue to close the gap to other midfield teams like Racing Bulls and Alpine, with the German identifying that “managing the tyres and making sure you get to the end” made the difference on a day when the three squads showed “identical pace”.

All the key moments from the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix

Someone else who seemed to thrive in the tyre department – at least until a poorly timed Virtual Safety Car unravelled his race – was McLaren’s Norris, who admitted that he was proud of his performance despite missing out on victory.

He said: “The way I drive, the way I can look after the tyres and get lap time out of it, it's giving me a lot of opportunities and I can do a better job than the others.”

La Monumental lived up to its name

Speaking of tyre management, few corners are as punishing on the Pirelli rubber as La Monumental, which – look away now if you hate puns – was undoubtedly a monumental feature of the circuit.

Standing at 550m long, flanked by up to 45,000 passionate fans, and with a banking gradient of up to 24%, this arena-style section was a treat to watch as drivers accelerated through – even if some weren’t particularly happy with the traffic.

The variety of racing lines caused tempers to flare, especially as La Monumental led to a thrilling blind crest, making the courage required to send it around there even more admirable.

Another twist in the title fight

It’s not often that you hear an F1 driver – some of the most ambitious, ruthless athletes in the world – concede that one of their biggest rivals deserved victory more than them, but that’s exactly what happened in Madrid.

Kimi Antonelli clinched his eighth win of the season to extend his advantage in the Drivers’ Championship to a colossal 81 points, and although he celebrated, he also said: “It’s good to win, but it doesn’t feel as good because I think Lando today deserved to win. But overall, you know, we’ll take it.”

It wasn’t exactly a fair review of his performance, which saw the 20-year-old start in second place before he got ahead of Norris during the pit stops. He then inherited the lead from Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, who gambled on a long opening stint before finally changing his tyres with fewer than 10 laps to go.

Was there any way for Norris to win in Madrid after the VSC?

Like most races, it was far from straightforward and Antonelli had to resist challenges from both Norris and Max Verstappen in order to reap the reward of his most comfortable position so far in the standings.

Perhaps the biggest revelation came from his team mate Russell, who shared his belief that he’s no longer “in the fight for the drivers’ title” after taking P5 at the Madring. Mercedes boss Toto Wolff didn’t quite agree, emphasising that anything could happen over the remaining rounds, and what looks like “a nice buffer” can rapidly shrink after a couple of crashes or retirements.

With Norris on a fantastic run of form, Ferrari consistently sticking close by, and Russell enjoying minimal pressure on his shoulders, the battle to be crowned the 2026 champion still rages on.

title: 8 moments you might have missed at the Spanish Grand Prix
excerpt:
Another race weekend and another masterclass from Kimi Antonelli, who won the Spanish Grand Prix in its first edition at the Madring.

An element of luck in the Virtual Safety Car timing allowed the Mercedes driver to move past McLaren’s Lando Norris, while a pit stop under the VSC also benefited Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who finished second behind the Italian youngster.

It was a solid race for Charles Leclerc of Ferrari, finishing fourth after leading the race for more than 30 laps, but home hero Carlos Sainz had to retire his Williams, while another Spaniard, Fernando Alonso of Aston Martin, finished only in 17th place.

However, the weekend in Spain’s capital has been equally full of action off track – here are some of the moments you might have missed.

Driving around Madrid in style

Madrid is hosting Formula 1 for the first time in more than four decades.

And Red Bull wanted to let the entire town know that Formula 1 was in town over the weekend, putting the 2012 World Championship-winning car RB8 back on track...quite literally.

The car was driven through Madrid’s rail tunnels on specially designed wheels as part of the On Rails project that began in the city six months ago. It will definitely be one of the enduring images of the maiden Grand Prix at the Madring.

A new look for Williams

A special Grand Prix required a special look – and Williams harked back to an old look, with a new livery and race suits inspired by their championship-winning car FW07C, which raced at Jarama, Madrid, in 1981.

The 1981 season saw a memorable performance from Williams, with the outfit taking home the Teams' honours with drivers Carlos Reutemann and Alan Jones taking second and third in the Drivers' Championship.

Whilst the 2026 running of the Spanish Grand Prix didn't go their way, it was still a future inspired by a great past.

Football enters the paddock…

It’s not possible to avoid the football world when in Madrid. Both past and current players made sure to leave their mark in the paddock over the weekend.

Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto of Alpine had a special chauffeur around Madrid – former Real Madrid player and manager, French legend Zinedine Zidane.

And former Spain internationals enjoyed some padel fun at Madring. Iker Casillas, Fernando Llorente and Raul Gonzalez joined Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton of Ferrari for a few rallies.

After that Hamilton and Leclerc also headed to the Santiago Bernabeu Stadium, home of Real Madrid, to show off some football skills.

Max Verstappen's paddock souvenir came courtesy of Atletico Madrid pair David Hancko and Jan Oblak, as the four-time World Champion scored one of their famed red-and-white stripped jerseys. Madrid was certainly the perfect place for a football-F1 crossover.

Goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois, midfielder Jude Bellingham, defender Trent Alexander-Arnold and forward Vinicius Jr were among those trading the Bernabéu for the Spanish Grand Prix paddock.

Accustomed to performing in front of packed stadiums, the football stars looked right at home, soaking up the atmosphere and joining the crowds eager to witness history as Formula 1 returned to the Spanish capital.

Spanish tennis royalty in the house

It wasn’t just football stars making their way through the paddock. With Formula 1 returning to Madrid for a landmark weekend, 22-time Grand Slam champion Rafael Nadal was never likely to miss the chance to witness a moment of sporting history in his home country.

The Spanish tennis legend was spotted at the circuit alongside his father, Sebastián Nadal, taking in the atmosphere as fans packed the venue for the long-awaited return of Grand Prix racing to the capital.

New chefs in the house!

Can you really spend time in Spain and not try to cook a tortilla? Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas had their own culinary moment in Madrid.

“Cheltteri” took on one of Spain’s most iconic culinary challenges: the tortilla flip. While it might look simple, flipping a Spanish tortilla without turning it into a scrambled mess requires plenty of confidence, technique and a steady hand.

Judging by their efforts, the pair had clearly been paying attention, showing off some impressive skills as they embraced the local culture away from the track. After a weekend in Spain, it seems they’ve become just as adept at flipping tortillas as they are at handling their Cadillac F1 machinery.

Special helmets for the Madring debut

As the Madring made its debut in Formula 1, several drivers wanted to mark the occasion with a custom-designed helmet for the weekend.

Alonso turned heads before a wheel had even been turned thanks to a special all-black helmet created by BOSS. A showcase of style meets speed, the helmet made for a bold fashion-forward statement from the two-time champ.

Sainz marked his home race with a helmet that was as much a tribute to his journey as it was to Spain itself. Wrapped in the colours of the Spanish flag, the special design celebrated the occasion of racing in Madrid while also looking back at the milestones that shaped his career.

References to his very first kart race in 2005 were woven into the artwork, alongside nods to the achievements of his father, two-time World Rally Champion Carlos Sainz Sr.

Norris took a different approach to his Madrid special helmet, collaborating with local artist Sandra Del Pilar and inviting her to "represent the city through her eyes".

The finished design was a striking mix of vivid colours and artistic flourishes inspired by Madrid's character, turning the McLaren driver's helmet into a colourful masterpiece.

An alpine skier with an Alpine driver?

Pierre Gasly found himself in good company in Madrid as he met Olympic and World Champion skier Bode Miller. The pair traded stories from their respective sports, comparing the thrill of carving through snow with the challenge of threading an F1 car through a high-speed corner.

While skis and race cars might seem worlds apart, it made for a fitting meeting between two competitors who have built careers on speed.

title: Lawson reflects on his Red Bull outings after sixth in Madrid
excerpt:
Liam Lawson believes "overall it's been a strong three weekends" with Red Bull since replacing the injured Isack Hadjar midway through the season.

The Kiwi made his third start for Red Bull this season in last weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, and achieved his best result since swapping his Racing Bulls machine by finishing sixth.

Lawson was one of the few drivers to make an overtake on the Madring street circuit, before making a late pit stop to claim his second points finish with Red Bull, having finished seventh in the Netherlands.

"Hard to overtake is really the biggest thing. We started on the hard [tyre] as well and with the Virtual Safety Car, it didn't really help us," Lawson told F1 TV about the challenges of Formula 1's newest venue.

"Made quite a risky pass on Franco [Colapinto] earlier on and felt like it was going to be really important for our race but then the VSC came out and they boxed anyway, so it didn't really make a difference.

"Was quite fun to do but this track is very difficult to pull it off [an overtake]. I didn't nearly make the corner and you do track limits you have to give the place back. Tough race."

Lawson's current performances with Red Bull are in stark contrast with the start of the 2025 season, where he competed in just two races before being demoted back to Racing Bulls.

Prior to his temporary move back to Red Bull, Lawson had scored points in eight out of 11 races so far this season, which was enough to earn another call-up to the senior team.

Although Hadjar was in the Madrid paddock over the weekend, the Frenchman's return from a wrist injury sustained over the summer break is still unknown, with Baku the next race in two weeks.

"I think so," said Lawson when asked if he was proud of his performances with Red Bull so far.

"I've just tried to maximise each weekend. Honestly, a lot of things coming into it were just driver specific that I knew were going to be challenging about this car, and just really tried to prepare as much as I could but it's been a very busy few weeks to be honest.

"Probably this coming week will be busy as well to be honest, I'll probably be doing prep for both cars again. It's just been a busy time trying to put everything together, but it's been good.

"I would have loved to have scored in Monza as well, but I think overall it's been a strong three weekends."

title: Mekies explains decision to ask Verstappen to give back places
excerpt:
Laurent Mekies has explained Red Bull's decision after the team told Max Verstappen to give back places at the start of the Spanish Grand Prix.

The four-time World Champion tangled with Lewis Hamilton after lights out at the start of the race in Madrid, as the Ferrari driver got ahead before Verstappen kept his P3 starting position, but only after cutting the first turn.

The Dutchman said on the radio that Hamilton “almost shunted him” and tried to resist team instructions to give the place back to avoid a potential penalty, especially after he had since overtaken Kimi Antonelli for P2.

After giving in and allowing both Antonelli and Hamilton through, he quickly returned to the top three after the Ferrari had a problem with its brakes, with the Briton forced to retire.

Verstappen was also able to make the most of a Virtual Safety Car period during his pit stop and eventually finished the race in P2 behind winner Antonelli.

Following Sunday's Grand Prix, Red Bull Team Principal Mekies was asked about the decision making progress and, while he admitted the team weren't expecting a "thank you email from Max in the car", they felt it was the right decision and "better to take the pain at that moment and to fight back after, rather than wait and risk a bigger penalty".

Speaking to F1 TV after the race, Verstappen explained the clash was just the nature of the track and, after the team decision, he just tried to do his race.

One further question put to Mekies was around the fact that Hamilton retired from the Grand Prix shortly after the decision was made for the place to be returned. However, the Red Bull boss insisted that, if they had waited, a bigger punishment could have been coming.

"We would have simply been penalized either five seconds or ten seconds at their discretion," he told F1 TV. "So that’s what would have happened. And of course, if you can imagine race scenarios with a Safety Car or other circumstances, it can cost you a lot more than a position or two."

He also went on to explain that he knew Verstappen would fight back and highlighted that he did so exceptionally well at the Madring.

"Luckily Max gave away the position before Lewis retired and ultimately continued to fight the race from that point," he continued. "Of course it is frustrating but, in fairness, I think P2 was the absolute best we could have achieved today."

Second place in the Spanish Grand Prix at the new Madring track leaves Verstappen sixth in the Drivers' Championship standings, with 145 points. P6 at Madrid for stand-in team mate Liam Lawson also sees Red Bull head to the next race weekend in Baku fourth in the Constructors' Championship.

title: Wolff on the challenge of unlocking Russell’s potential
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has explained how Mercedes need to work with George Russell to "unleash his potential” after he endured another setback in the title fight in Madrid, with team mate Kimi Antonelli outscoring him once again.

Russell was open about his struggles with tyre degradation over the weekend at the new circuit, which contributed to him missing out on the fight for pole position and settling for sixth place in Qualifying.

From there, the team executed a two-stop strategy to switch the Briton onto medium tyres under the Virtual Safety Car, and back to a second set of hards later in the race. Russell questioned the decision at first, but later admitted that it didn’t significantly impact his final result of P5.

Although he finished close behind Charles Leclerc, there was a gap of nearly 30s to race winner Antonelli, who has subsequently increased his lead over Russell to 81 points in the Drivers’ Championship.

“You can see the pace he had towards the end when he was catching Leclerc,” Wolff said. “You know that he was fastest out on track but after the tyre changes, the pace wasn't there and I just don't know where it is. We have to analyse it because clearly it's in him, it's in the car and we just have to unlock it.

“When it comes to George, you can have good races, bad races, good years and bad years, but we're talking about the driver that has won everything that you could have potentially won before.

“Every single karting championship, Formula 3 in his rookie year, Formula 2 in his rookie year, went into the Williams. I mean, we're talking about a top driver.

“We need to find out what it is for him to be able to unleash that potential, and of course there's the psychological side. If you have a run like him this year you're taking a beating but the great ones, they recover and I think that George has all he needs to fight for championships.”

With Antonelli’s significant advantage over Russell and rivals like Lewis Hamilton, who now sits 101 points adrift following his retirement from the Spanish Grand Prix, Mercedes are in a comfortable position heading into the remaining rounds.

Russell effectively ruled himself out of the championship battle after Sunday’s result, but Wolff was adamant that the situation can change at any given moment, especially with nine rounds to go.

“It's a mechanical sport,” the Team Principal explained. “You can DNF, you can crash out and it happens two times in a row and then suddenly what looked like a nice buffer is not anymore because you have six races to go.

“So in my opinion, we just need to ignore the points until it is mathematically not realistic anymore, or not real anymore for them to win, and until then just concentrate on each and every weekend, try to bring your best game.

“2027 [development] started a while ago already, long before the summer. We switched resources into the next year and that continues as per the plan, independent of where we're standing in the championship.”

title: Piastri assesses his ‘painful’ Spanish GP in Madrid
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri had a race to forget in Madrid after a first lap incident derailed his afternoon on a day where Lando Norris showed the McLaren had the pace to fight for the win.

The Australian finished down in eighth place, behind the Alpine of Franco Colapinto, and while the unlucky timing of the Virtual Safety Car prevented his team mate from fighting for the win, Piastri had his own slice of misfortune.

He picked up damage to his front wing after first lap contact with George Russell’s Mercedes, with the Australian left nowhere to go as the Mercedes ducked across the track towards the barriers. That left him with aero damage in the form of a broken end-plate and short on downforce, something the team could only mitigate but not fully fix at his one and only pit stop.

And having started on the hard tyres, the timing of the early Virtual Safety Car also proved problematic for the 25-year-old.

“It was pretty painful obviously, from Lap 1," he assessed afterwards. "Yeah, not much I really could have done from there.

"The timing for the VSC was certainly not ideal for us, [stayed] on the hard and it was just a difficult afternoon."

Having opted not to stop under the VSC, Piastri ran a long opening stint in the hopes of a later VSC, Safety Car or red flag moment. But no more incidents came, leaving him to make a pit stop under full racing conditions.

The time lost meant he came out in traffic and, while he pulled off one of the few overtakes on Sunday, picking off Arvid Lindblad, Piastri could not find a way past the Alpine of Colapinto late on.

To trace back the difficulties Piastri faced, you have to look to Qualifying where he needed an extra set of softs to guarantee he made it through Q2. That left him as the only front runner to have a used set of the C4 tyre for his first run in Q3.

On his second run on the new tyres, where balance would have been different to the used set, he made a mistake early in his lap and from there, could only qualify seventh.

That left him starting in the midst of the pack, something always fraught with danger as all the cars barrel down into Turn 1 on a narrow street track.

“It was mostly the end of Qualifying and then Lap 1 obviously was far from ideal, having damage for the whole race,” he explained.

“It was tough like that, but today we just tried to learn as much as we could to try and get more out of the car and the way I drive it. Hopefully we’ve learned a few things for the rest of the year.”

Piastri has two podiums to show for his 2026 season, the last of which came in Miami, and one top-three finish in a Sprint. His team mate has five rostrums, including two victories, a Sprint win, three other Sprint top-three finishes, three pole positions and a Sprint pole.

The contrast between their two seasons is stark, and is further highlighted in the Championship where Norris has amassed 66 more points than his team mate.

Piastri will be hoping his luck changes soon, and he has a chance to set things right next time out in Azerbaijan. Last year it was the event that saw his championship hopes dealt their first big blow after an early DNF - something he will want to atone for when the F1 paddock reconvenes in Baku in two weeks' time.

title: Why Vasseur believes Ferrari had the pace to win in Madrid
excerpt:
Fred Vasseur was confident that Charles Leclerc could’ve won the Spanish Grand Prix if an incident had disrupted the latter stages of the race, with the Ferrari Team Principal believing that “the potential is there” for the team.

Leclerc qualified fifth and gained an early position from the retirement of his team mate Lewis Hamilton, but unlike those around him, he and the team opted not to pit for fresh tyres when the Virtual Safety Car was deployed.

As a result, he inherited the lead and maintained a consistent gap to Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli, with Ferrari hoping that the race would see a red flag or Safety Car to give Leclerc what would essentially be a free pit stop.

Unfortunately, that didn’t materialise and he was finally called in after spending nearly 50 laps on the hard compound, dropping him out of podium contention. He eventually crossed the line 29.116s behind Antonelli and narrowly held off George Russell for P4.

“You see that you always have positives and negatives, it doesn't matter the weekend,” Vasseur said. “The pace of Charles in the race was more than good – we did a stint of 49 laps I think with the hard and the pace was still there.

“All the teams did the same with one car on softs or mediums and another one on hards to cover all the options. He was leading the group of [drivers on] hards and I think with a second incident, a red flag, it was the win.

“A Safety Car, it would have been P2, P3. It's more a strategy than something else and on his side, the pace was good. It's the only thing that we can do on Sunday. If we missed something, it's more yesterday [in Qualifying]. Today I think we did what we had to do – we took the risks we had to take and the pace is the pace that we need to have.”

While Leclerc was able to demonstrate Ferrari’s strength in race trim, Hamilton only lasted a short time before a brake issue forced him to retire the car, marking his first DNF of the season.

The Briton enjoyed a fantastic launch to instantly challenge Max Verstappen for P3, with the Dutchman offering him the position after he cut the first corner. However, Hamilton quickly began to drop back as he reported that the brake pedal was going long and he couldn’t stop the car.

He did manage to make it safely back to the garage, where he was left to rue the missed opportunity, telling Sky Sports F1: “I think we had the car to fight for a win today, and unfortunately it just didn't work out.”

Asked whether the problem was caused by a small brush with the wall, Vasseur replied: “Obviously I don't know, because they were working on the car when I left. The pedal was long on the end of Lap 1, I think, and we tried to fix it from the pit wall, and then it happened again a couple of corners later, and at this kind of track it makes no sense to take a crazy risk.

“There were still 56 [laps to go]. The first time it happened was from Lap 2 and it was too risky.”

title: Honda announce changes to leadership of power unit programme
excerpt:
Honda have announced that they will make changes to the leadership of their Formula 1 power unit development programme.

Monday's announcement confirmed that Yoichiro Fukao, currently serving as Deputy Leader of the F1 Project, would take over the role of Large Project Leader from October 1, succeeding Tetsushi Kakuda who has led the programme to date.

"This organisational change is a planned transition designed to ensure the reliable transfer of technical expertise to the next generation of engineers," read a statement from Honda.

"Following the introduction of the new regulations in 2026, and with further regulatory changes expected from 2027 onwards, Honda aims to establish a robust development framework and deliver a highly competitive PU by transitioning to the new structure at an early stage."

The Japanese manufacturer has endured a difficult time under the new-for-2026 regulations as an engine supplier to Aston Martin.

The Silverstone-based team have generally been at the back of the field throughout the campaign, with the Honda power unit suffering from both a lack of power and reliability compared to their rivals.

Aston Martin sit only above F1 debutants Cadillac in the teams' standings, with Fernando Alonso scoring three points across two races, while Lance Stroll has yet to score.

At last weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, Stroll retired with brake issues, while Alonso managed to reach the chequered flag at his home event two laps down in P17.

Fukao has been with Honda since 2002, beginning with the development of engine and gearbox control systems before pivoting to Honda's involvement in MotoGP between 2009-2011.

Having then focused on the development of hybrid systems over the next three years, Fukao went back to F1, eventually becoming Deputy Leader of the F1 Project in 2017 and again in 2022 as Honda looked to return to the sport.

title: The 2026 Qualifying and race head-to-heads so far
excerpt:
As the 2026 season continues, F1.com assesses how the team mate head-to-heads have stacked up so far. Who from each of the 11 pairings on the grid has had the upper hand in Qualifying and/or race trim across the campaign? Let’s take a look at the numbers…

Mercedes

Qualifying: Russell 6-8 Antonelli

Race: Russell 4-10 Antonelli

Perhaps unsurprisingly given his hold on the top spot in the Drivers’ Championship, Kimi Antonelli has also taken the lead when it comes to the head-to-head statistics at Mercedes. The Italian has beaten George Russell in Qualifying eight times out of 14, with six of those occasions seeing him take pole position.

The numbers are similar in the race day figures, Antonelli having crossed the line ahead of Russell at 10 Grands Prix – and winning at eight of them. Russell on the other hand has experienced marginally more bad luck, recording two DNFs in comparison to one for Antonelli.

Antonelli's most recent win was last weekend in the Spanish Grand Prix, with Russell finishing fifth and losing further ground in the title race.

Ferrari

Qualifying: Leclerc 7-7 Hamilton

Race: Leclerc 6-8 Hamilton

Over at Ferrari, there is little to choose between Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton on both counts. Hamilton just edged Leclerc as the pair started P4 and P5 for the Spanish Grand Prix, putting them level in Qualifying.

But after Hamilton suffered a brake issue and retired in Spain, Leclerc's fourth means he has edged closer on head-to-head in the races, with Hamilton just beating Leclerc in terms of podiums scored by five to four.

McLaren

Qualifying: Norris 9-5 Piastri

Race: Norris 8-5 Piastri*

*No mark included for the Chinese Grand Prix as both drivers failed to start

In the Qualifying statistics between Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, Norris leads the way with nine better results. This includes his pole positions at the Hungarian and Dutch Grands Prix, and more recently starting from the front in Spain.

The McLaren pair aren't too far apart in race day figures, but they are even in terms of non-scores – Norris having recorded two DNFs, while Piastri has one to his name as well as a DNS from the season opener in Australia (not including the Chinese Grand Prix where both recorded a DNS). Norris is responsible for the squad's two victories so far at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort.

Red Bull

Qualifying: Verstappen 8-3 Hadjar

Qualifying: Verstappen 3-0 Lawson

Race: Verstappen 8-3 Hadjar

Race: Verstappen 2-1 Lawson

Isack Hadjar faced the difficult task of stepping up as Max Verstappen’s new team mate at Red Bull in 2026 – and while he has enjoyed a solid start to the campaign, it is the Dutchman that leads the way in the statistics.

Verstappen has outqualified his team mate on eight occasions, as well as finishing ahead on race day the same number of times. The four-time World Champion recorded retirements at the other three events, one more DNF than the two experienced by Hadjar.

The Frenchman was unexpectedly replaced by Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson for the Dutch Grand Prix after sustaining a wrist injury, and while Verstappen narrowly beat the New Zealander in Qualifying, he suffered a massive crash at the start of the race to mark his fourth DNF of the season.

Lawson brought it home in seventh place, scoring points on his first appearance for the team since he was demoted shortly into the 2025 season.

Lawson remained with Red Bull for the Italian Grand Prix, but was handed the tough ask of recovering from a pit lane start after a raft of PU penalties were applied to his car. The Kiwi put in a better performance in Spain and took his best result with the team in P6, but once again finished behind Verstappen.

Racing Bulls

Qualifying: Lawson 6-5 Lindblad

Qualifying: Tsunoda 0-3 Lindblad

Race: Lawson 8-3 Lindblad

Race: Tsunoda 1-2 Lindblad

The first half of the season has been strong for Racing Bulls, with both drivers performing well. However, it is Lawson who has taken the lead in the head-to-heads, albeit narrowly in Qualifying form – the New Zealander holding the edge by six to five over Arvid Lindblad.

Lawson has finished ahead of Lindblad at eight out of the 11 Grands Prix they have contested for Racing Bulls, though the gap between the duo – who have recorded five double points finishes so far – has often been small. There has been one retirement so far for Lawson (in Miami), while Lindblad did not start in Canada due to a clutch issue.

Their run of seven rounds with at least one driver in the top 10 came to an end in Zandvoort, where reserve driver Yuki Tsunoda stepped in for Lawson. The Japanese racer had never driven the 2026 cars before, making it even more impressive that he came close to scoring as he improved from P12 on the grid – two positions behind Lindblad – to P11.

Tsunoda remained with the team in Monza and did add a point to their tally, with Lindblad also returning to the top 10 in what proved a strong weekend for the team.

Lindblad was once again in the points last weekend at the Madring with P9 having out-qualifed Tsunoda, who finished the race in P14.

Alpine

Qualifying: Gasly 11-3 Colapinto

Race: Gasly 9-5 Colapinto

Pierre Gasly has been dominant in the Qualifying statistics at Alpine, having beaten Franco Colapinto by 11 to three.

He even grabbed his maiden pole position at Monza, completely on merit in a dry session as the upgraded Alpine took the fight to the top teams.

The picture is a little more even on race day, where Gasly’s lead is now nine over Colapinto’s five. The French driver could not back up his pole position at Monza with a podium, but did come home seventh with his team mate also scoring in ninth.

Colapinto got the better of Gasly in both Qualifying and the race in Madrid, starting P9 and reaching the chequered flag in P7.

Haas

Qualifying: Bearman 9-5 Ocon

Race: Bearman 8-5 Ocon*

*No mark for the Dutch Grand Prix as both drivers retired

At Haas, Ollie Bearman has qualified ahead of Esteban Ocon on nine occasions. The Briton’s best Saturday result so far was a P10 in China, which also marked the only time that one of the squad’s cars has progressed to Q3.

Bearman has the edge in Grand Prix finishes too, beating Ocon by eight to five. In terms of reliability, Bearman has suffered four DNFs, with Ocon experiencing his first of the year in Zandvoort as neither were able to finish the race.

Audi

Qualifying: Hulkenberg 7-7 Bortoleto

Race: Hulkenberg 6-8 Bortoleto

Audi drivers Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto are evenly matched when it comes to Qualifying performances, with Bortoleto claiming their best starting position of P8 at the Belgian Grand Prix.

It is also Bortoleto who has the better race day statistics, the Brazilian finishing ahead of Hulkenberg at eight of the 14 rounds so far. The younger driver has enjoyed better luck in terms of reliability; Bortoleto has crossed the line at every race barring China – where he failed to start – while Hulkenberg has suffered three DNFs along with a DNS in Australia.

Hulkenberg got the better of Bortoleto in both Qualifying and the race in Spain, securing P10 and scoring one point for Audi in the process.

Williams

Qualifying: Albon 4-10 Sainz

Race: Albon 6-8 Sainz

It has been a tough campaign so far for Williams, who remain down in P9 of the Teams’ Championship. While there has not been much to celebrate, Carlos Sainz might take heart from the fact that he has led the Qualifying head-to-head by 10 to four over Alex Albon.

That does not quite tell the full story though, with Albon offering his team mate a tow in Monza to ensure Sainz made it to Q2.

Sainz also tops the Grand Prix figures, by eight to six. Points have been a rarity for the team, with the Spaniard recording three P9 finishes while Albon has a P8 and a P10 to his name.

Aston Martin

Qualifying: Alonso 12-2 Stroll

Race: Alonso 8-2 Stroll*

*No mark for the Australian, Chinese, Barcelona and Italian Grands Prix as both drivers retired

Like Williams, Aston Martin have endured a challenging 2026. Such were the squad’s car issues that neither driver was able to finish the opening two rounds in Australia and China, while both also retired with reliability problems in Barcelona. However, substantial upgrades to the car and power unit have offered encouraging signs of progress.

In terms of the head-to-heads, Fernando Alonso has outscored Lance Stroll on both counts – albeit by a lesser extent on Sundays – and the Spaniard is also responsible for the team’s three points as he finished P10 in Monaco and P9 in the Netherlands.

Cadillac

Qualifying: Perez 7-7 Bottas

Race: Perez 8-4 Bottas*

*No mark for the Austrian and Hungarian Grands Prix as both drivers retired

Cadillac recruited the experienced pairing of Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez for the squad’s maiden F1 season – and while the duo have often been fighting towards the rear of the pack, Perez got the better of Bottas in Spain and drew level on their Qualifying figures so far.

However, the Mexican holds the advantage in the Grand Prix statistics, finishing ahead of Bottas on eight occasions. Both drivers have suffered their fair share of reliability concerns, with the Finn retiring from six races while Perez is on five DNFs.

title: Max Verstappen seriously considered quitting F1
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has revealed that he seriously considered walking away from Formula 1 altogether before eventually putting pen to paper on a new Red Bull deal through 2030.

The four-time F1 champion's previous contract had run through 2028, but the Dutchman opted to commit to the Milton Keynes-based team for four more seasons, despite talk of a possible switch elsewhere or even a premature retirement.

Speaking to Bild, Verstappen confirmed that talks with McLaren had taken place amid Red Bull's struggles this campaign, albeit thoughts of leaving F1 entirely were uppermost in his mind.

"You have to take every conversation with another team seriously," Verstappen said. "But in the end, I was closer to quitting Formula 1 than to signing with another racing team."

Asked just how close he came to calling time on his career, Verstappen laughed before explaining his thinking.

"You either quit or you don't, so it's a 50/50 decision," he said. "I seriously considered calling it quits. But at the end of the day, I just love racing."

[Article continues below]

Naturally, given everything Verstappen has achieved in the sport, he knows he has nothing "to prove to myself".

He added: "I'm a four-time world champion, and after my first title, I'd already achieved everything I ever wanted.

"I don't race for the history books, but for myself, the team, and our fans. Because of that, the decision was ultimately made quickly."

Verstappen, currently sixth in the drivers' standings on 145 points, a staggering 147 behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli, insisted the timing of his new deal with Red Bull reflected a straightforward outlook rather than any external pressure.

"If both parties want to work together long-term, why wait?" he said. "The criticism doesn't bother me. I don't care what others think of me.

"The only thing that matters is how my family, my management, the team, and I feel about it. I have to be able to get along with myself, and I can."

Unlike 45-year-old Fernando Alonso, however, Verstappen does not expect to still be racing in Formula 1 come his mid-40s.

"I don't think so, but that's impossible to predict," he said. "I'll keep racing as long as I enjoy it."

title: Carlos Sainz accuses Fernando Alonso of getting him Madring penalty
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz feels that Fernando Alonso's indignation over team radio earned him his five-second time penalty after the compatriots clashed at the Spanish Grand Prix.

Approaching the hazardous Turn 5-6 chicane on Lap 12 at the Madring, Alonso was attacking Sainz on the outside in the battle for P17 when the Williams moved across, initiating contact between the pair.

The Aston Martin driver immediately vented his frustration, saying "He squeezed me into the wall" after sustaining damage to his front wing.

Sainz, however, felt Alonso had made more out of it than needed, suggesting it was the two-time F1 drivers' champion's radio communications that had swayed race control and the stewards into punishing him.

"Nothing to say, really," the Williams driver told media, including RacingNews365. "It's the nature of that corner when you turn right, and I think he complained on the radio, so he managed to get me a penalty.

"Like always, the nature of that corner is always going to lead to these kinds of crashes because there's only space for one; there's not even space for two.

"And you cannot keep looking in your mirror while you're turning and looking and doing a right-left because you need to look forward.

"So at one point you need to focus on your own driving line, and yeah, I don't think Fernando was alongside me or anything."

Alonso: Sainz incident was 'unnecessary'

Alonso, however, was satisfied with the decision after what he deemed to be an "unnecessary" collision in front of their shared home fans.

"He had a penalty, so if they [the stewards] consider that enough, it's good for me," he added when told that Sainz had played it down.

"We didn't finish any of the two in the points, but I think that was unnecessary.

"There was plenty of room on the left. I was just on the wall on the right, 340 kph; I think it was not needed."

title: F1 champion loses £1.4 million court battle
excerpt:
1979 F1 drivers' champion Jody Scheckter has lost a court battle over a £1.4m tax bill following the failure of his organic buffalo farming business.

Former Formula 1 world champion Jody Scheckter has lost a high-profile court battle against HM Revenue and Customs over a £1.4m tax bill connected to his organic buffalo farming business.

The 76-year-old South African, who won the 1979 World F1 drivers' championship with Ferrari, had challenged a backdated demand for £1,457,634 after an HMRC inspector ruled that his farming partnership had wrongly offset losses against profits from other parts of his business between 2008 and 2010.

Scheckter purchased Laverstoke Park in Overton, Hampshire, after relocating to England with his wife Clare in 1996, subsequently investing £55m of his personal fortune into the estate and around 3,000 acres of surrounding land.

The venture, which supplied organic meat to Ocado and specialised in buffalo mozzarella, closed its dairy and buffalo farming operations in 2024, citing significant increases in costs and a reduction in milk volumes.

The seven-figure losses incurred by the LLP Laverstoke Farm Produce had been set off against taxes owed on other income through a mechanism known as sideways loss relief.

HMRC declared the arrangement invalid in 2019 and issued the demand for repayment. The relief is available to farmers, but only where the enterprise becomes profitable within five years of being established.

The Laverstoke farming partnership registered a loss in almost every year since it was founded, meaning it failed to satisfy that requirement.

Driver

Jody Scheckter

South African

Judge: 'Considerable sadness' over failed venture

Dismissing Scheckter's appeal at the First-tier Tribunal, Judge Tony Beare said it was impossible to have been involved in the case without feeling "considerable sadness" at how the project had turned out.

The judge acknowledged that Scheckter "was extremely passionate about the positive effects which healthier eating would engender for everyone" and said the tribunal expressed its "profound regret for the way that things developed."

Scheckter, who competed in Formula 1 between 1972 and 1980 and won ten grands prix across nine seasons, is still the only African to have won a Formula 1 world championship.

After retiring from motorsport, he founded Firearms Training Systems, a weapons simulation business whose revenues exceeded £100m by the early 1990s, before channelling much of that wealth into Laverstoke Park.

The judge stressed that Scheckter did not fall into the category of a hobby farmer seeking to avoid tax on other income, but ruled that the losses for the three relevant years could not lawfully be offset under the Income Tax (Trading and Other Income) Act 2005.

title: Lando Norris left counting brutal cost of VSC math as Kimi Antonelli tightens F1 title grip
excerpt:
It was a case of small margins that cost Lando Norris and helped Kimi Antonelli.

14 September 2:50PM

Lando Norris lost the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix by a five-second margin he had no say in, and with it, most of what remained of his F1 drivers' title defence.

Norris took pole by 0.011s from Kimi Antonelli on Saturday with a lap described by McLaren team principal Andrea Stella as "a masterpiece".

He then led comfortably until lap 15, when Lance Stroll stopped his Aston Martin at Turn 20. The virtual safety car was deployed two seconds after Norris had passed the pit entry.

Behind him, Mercedes driver Antonelli and Red Bull's Max Verstappen pitted into the neutralised phase; Norris had to run another lap and stopped just as the VSC ended, paying the full price where his rivals paid almost none.

McLaren then compounded the situation. A seven-second stop under green-flag conditions, due to issues with the right-front wheel, dropped the Briton to fifth, and on a circuit where overtaking barely exists, his recovery to third was the ceiling.

He crossed the line 5.089s behind Antonelli and 0.738s behind Verstappen. It was a stomach-punch result for Norris.

"There was nothing I could do," he said. "Congrats to Kimi. Luck was not on our side."

"I gave it a good fight to try and catch up to Max, but [it was] difficult to pass. He didn't make any mistakes... yeah, a tough race. One that got away from us."

Explaining how things unfolded, he added: "The VSC came out after I was already round the last corner. The others were very fortunate today, or I was unfortunate, whichever way around you want to look at it.

"Of course, I believe I deserved it. We did a very good job. I feel like I did everything right this weekend, so for it to be lost like this is just pretty crappy."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lando Norris

British

1

The call McLaren could not make

Stella conceded the pit stop was McLaren's own doing, but framed the wider loss as timing.

"Starting from pole position, leading the race and having incredible pace… this would've been a race won by many seconds, and we ended up in third position," he said.

"The reality is that in racing, there are elements that you can control and some that you cannot control. The timing of the virtual safety car was a couple of seconds too late.

"Lando had already passed the pit entry, and then he was a few seconds too early because then it was ending once he came in to pit."

The obvious counter is that McLaren could have pitted pre-emptively under the yellows. Stella did not dismiss it, but explained why the sums are brutal.

"Here, the problem is that you need to be extremely careful because it is 27 seconds if you don't pit under a virtual safety car," he said. "So if you get it wrong, it will be extremely penalising."

That is the mechanism worth understanding. At a circuit that the Madring's designers built around the IFEMA halls, with angled braking zones and barriers close enough to punish any adjustment, track position was effectively the result.

Oscar Piastri's afternoon proved it from a different perspective: front-wing endplate damage from lap-one contact with George Russell, a flap adjustment rather than a wing change to save time, and then a release into a four-car train. He finished eighth.

[Article continues below]

© Mercedes F1

Antonelli's cushion

Antonelli's eighth win of the campaign leaves him on 292 points, 81 clear of team-mate Russell and 106 ahead of Norris in fourth.

Even Antonelli conceded the day was not his on merit: "It's good to win, but it doesn't feel as good because I think Lando deserved to win."

Toto Wolff was more blunt about the reason. "I think we've been mostly unlucky with VSCs and safety cars this year. Here the race god was with us, and we were able to pull him in when the VSC came out," the Mercedes boss said.

The uncomfortable reading for McLaren is that Madrid was a maximum weekend, pole and the fastest car, converted into 15 points while the leader took 25. Norris does not need better luck so much as a run of Antonelli failures, and the Italian is not offering any.

"Of course, yes, I have a big lead, but you never know what can happen," Antonelli said. "So I just need to be ready for anything and keep maximising every opportunity I get. Then we'll see where we end up at the end of the year."

At this stage, it is fast becoming a case of when, and not if, Antonelli becomes F1 drivers' champion this season.

title: Kimi Antonelli makes 'aggressive' concession after 'undeserved' triumph
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has acknowledged being "too aggressive" at the start of the Spanish Grand Prix, which the Mercedes driver felt left him in a "bad position" to recover from.

Antonelli ultimately took victory at the Madring from Max Verstappen and Lando Norris, but only after the forgiving timing of the virtual safety car, which essentially ruined the McLaren's race.

Having lined up alongside the MCL40 on the front row of the grid, Antonelli attempted to seize the lead through the first corner, but went in too hot and had to skip the second corner.

After relinquishing the position to Norris, he made the same mistake again at Turn 5. This time, he fell behind Verstappen too as he feathered out the throttle.

Fortunately for the Italian, the Red Bull driver had to concede second and third place — to Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton, whom he passed off track — to avoid being penalised.

Despite having no answer for Norris' pace, the 20-year-old eventually assumed the lead when the reigning F1 drivers' champion was denied a cheap pit stop under the Lance Stroll-induced VSC.

From there, it was a matter of biding his time, with overtaking all but impossible at F1's newest circuit, rendering much of the afternoon a foregone conclusion.

"It’s good to win, and I think the pace at the end was good," Antonelli told media, including RacingNews365, whilst reflecting on the result.

"But if I have to be realistic and honest, today we didn’t deserve to win. Lando deserved to win today, and so I think our result was probably P2 or even P3.

"I just didn’t do a good enough job at the start, being a bit too aggressive and then putting myself in a bad position. So definitely things to work on. But all in all, it went well, and I’m happy with that. But yeah, we’re just going to try to be better in Baku."

Antonelli: Things to review after bailing out of risky move

Expanding on the frenetic opening corners of an otherwise damp squib of an afternoon in the Spanish capital, Antonelli shared his perspective from the cockpit of his W17

The now eight-time grand prix winner admitted his approach left him in an "awkward position" after opting to avoid a potential collision with Norris.

"I did try [to overtake], but obviously, Lando is not going to let me pass by; he did what he had to do," Antonelli explained.

"I found myself cutting the chicane twice. In the second chicane, I thought I could maybe make it, but I felt like it was too risky also for contact.

"So I decided to bail out. And then I was a bit in an awkward position because then Max could overtake me on the outside in seven. So definitely things to review, but it was still a great team effort."

title: Racing Bulls respond to Audi appeal as Yuki Tsunoda faces jeopardy
excerpt:
Racing Bulls boss Alan Permane is looking forward to a second trip to Paris after Audi appealed the stewards' decision not to penalise Yuki Tsunoda at Monza.

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane has addressed Audi's appeal against the stewards' decision not to punish Yuki Tsunoda for a start infringement at the Italian Grand Prix.

The German marque initially lodged its intention with the FIA after Tsunoda scored a point at Monza, with confirmation coming on media day for the Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring.

Following Charles Leclerc's red flag-triggering crash, Tsunoda lined up P14, but initially approached the wrong side of the grid before correcting his line and stopping in his allocated box.

His car was left at an angle towards the pit wall, prompting race director Rui Marques to abort the restart and order an additional formation lap. Under Article B5.9.4 of the sporting regulations, a driver deemed responsible for an extra formation lap must normally enter the pit lane and restart from there.

However, the stewards found Tsunoda had remained within his grid box and that the decision to run another formation lap was Marques' call.

Crucially, Racing Bulls had not been informed that Tsunoda was considered responsible, meaning it had no reason to instruct him to pit. The stewards therefore ruled that the extra lap resulted from the race director's assessment rather than being directly caused by Tsunoda.

Audi disagrees with that interpretation and stands to gain a point if the appeal succeeds. Gabriel Bortoleto finished P11, seven seconds behind Tsunoda, so overturning the decision would promote the Brazilian driver into P10 and hand him the final point.

"We raised a concern regarding the application of Article B5.9.4, which requires a driver who causes an extra formation lap to enter the pit lane and resume the race from there," Audi said in a statement. "The stewards issued a decision of No Further Action, and we have notified our intention to appeal."

Permane reacts to the appeal

Permane's response, meanwhile, came with a hint of humour. The Racing Bulls boss is set for another trip to Paris after the team's involvement in the FIA International Court of Appeal's recent hearing over the Monaco Grand Prix, where McLaren and Red Bull successfully appealed the reinstatement of Pierre Gasly's penalties.

That hearing took place in late August, with the decision published on 3 September during the Italian Grand Prix weekend.

"Well, it’s always nice to have a night out in Paris, first of all, or a second one in quick succession," Permane joked to media, including RacingNews365. "Look, we’ll go there, obviously, and defend the team and defend Yuki.

"I can’t really go into it more than that while it’s still an open case. Well, actually, it’s not even an open case yet because I don’t think it’s been… We haven’t even had a notification from the FIA to say.

"But I’m sure that will go ahead, and I guess, at some point in late October, we’ll head to Paris."

title: Former F1 driver issues apology after McLaren misunderstanding
excerpt:
Former Renault/Lotus and Haas F1 driver Romain Grosjean has taken to social media to apologise to McLaren Racing chief executive Zak Brown after misinterpreting remarks over the Spanish Grand Prix weekend.

Romain Grosjean has issued a public apology after misrepresenting comments made by McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown about Oscar Piastri during the Spanish Grand Prix weekend.

The former Formula 1 driver was on commentary duty for French television channel Canal+ throughout the event in Madrid.

During his broadcast on Sunday, Grosjean referenced an interview Brown had given on F1TV's post-qualifying show the previous evening, describing the McLaren chief's remarks as leaving him speechless and characterising them as a pointed attack on Piastri's performance.

He went as far as to claim Brown had said Norris was a world champion and simply the better driver.

The comments spread rapidly on social media, becoming one of the talking points of race day.

Article continues below.

What Brown actually said about Piastri

The F1TV interview in question featured Brown alongside presenters Laura Winter, Grosjean himself, and former F1 drivers Juan Pablo Montoya and Jolyon Palmer.

When Winter asked for Brown's reaction to Lando Norris taking pole position, the McLaren chief was effusive in his praise for the reigning F1 drivers' champion.

"The whole lap was amazing and Lando's just getting better and better and better," Brown told them. "When you see a lap like that put down, you just go, 'he's a world champion'."

When Montoya then asked what Piastri, who had qualified seventh while Norris took pole, needed to do to close the gap in qualifying, Brown's response was measured rather than dismissive.

"I think a) you got Lando on his A-plus game, right? So I don't think there was anything left laptime-wise there. So he found that," Brown said.

"Oscar's been right there with him all weekend and just didn't get that same extra lap. We'll continue to look at it. He'll look at the data and probably do what we all did and go, 'wow, what a lap' as well."

Article continues below.

Grosjean apologises to Brown and McLaren

By Sunday evening, Grosjean had taken to social media to set the record straight and acknowledge that he had badly misjudged Brown's words.

"Today, I made a comment on Canal+ regarding Zak Brown's comments about Oscar Piastri during an interview yesterday on F1TV, which I was part of," Grosjean wrote.

"I completely misunderstood his words and want to apologise for that. I know how important it is to Zak and the entire McLaren team to respect their drivers and treat them fairly and equally."

Grosjean also took the opportunity to reflect on McLaren's race day in Madrid, where the team lost a likely victory after Norris was caught out by the timing of a virtual safety car period.

"McLaren had the fastest car today and were unlucky with the VSC," he added. "I'm sure both Lando and Oscar will have another chance to fight for the win in Baku."

title: Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend set for another major schedule change
excerpt:
The Baku City Circuit will host yet another unconventional weekend later this month after FIA Formula 2 confirmed a "supersized" round featuring two qualifying sessions and two feature races.

The F1 race itself was already moved from Sunday to Saturday to avoid clashing with Azerbaijan's Remembrance Day on 27 September, shifting the entire programme forward by a day.

Now F2's Round 12 will follow suit with a considerably expanded format, marking the only time this season the feeder series will stage more than one feature race in a single weekend.

As the sole support series at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, F2 will run a 45-minute free practice session on Thursday morning, followed by two consecutive 20-minute qualifying sessions on Thursday afternoon.

The sprint race and first feature race will take place on Friday, with a second feature race on Saturday morning ahead of the grand prix.

Championship leader Nikola Tsolov holds a slender seven-point advantage over Rafael Câmara heading into Baku, with Gabriele Minì a further 17 points adrift.

With two feature races each carrying the full 25-point haul for a win, plus fastest-lap points and pole position awards from both qualifying sessions, the expanded weekend could prove pivotal.

FIA Formula 2 CEO Bruno Michel said: "As Formula 2 is the only Support Event at the Azerbaijan Formula 1 Grand Prix, together with the promoters, we have opted for a supersized F2 race weekend, with one Free Practice, two Qualifying sessions, one Sprint Race and two Feature Races."

He added: "This is the only weekend where the timetable allows the additional sessions, which will increase the level of entertainment even further for the attending crowd and all our fans. The Baku City Circuit always provides us with amazing racing, so we're very pleased to make the 12th Round of our season pretty unique."

End-of-season uncertainty lingers

Michel confirmed that the final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will revert to the standard format of one qualifying, one sprint race and one feature race.

However, there remains significant uncertainty over whether those events will go ahead at all.

The Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix remain officially on the 2026 F1 calendar, but contingency plans are in place should the regional security situation force cancellations.

Imola has been widely reported as a potential European replacement venue for a December season finale, though F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali has described it only as one option that is "not defined."

Whether F2 would also race at a potential Imola round is unclear, adding a further layer of unpredictability to a title battle that Baku could blow wide open.

title: Lando Norris Spanish heartbreak as Kimi Antonelli capitalises again - Spanish GP Winners and Losers
excerpt:
Check out RacingNews365's Winners and Losers from the first Spanish Grand Prix held at the Madring, won by championship leader Kimi Antonelli.

Kimi Antonelli won the inaugural Madrid race from second on the grid, but the decisive moment of the Spanish Grand Prix was a virtual safety car that arrived two seconds too late for Lando Norris.

Norris had converted pole into the lead and controlled the opening stint until Lance Stroll stopped on Lap 15.

Race Control neutralised the race just after the McLaren had passed the pit entry, and the VSC ended as Norris finally came in, costing him around 20 seconds against rivals who stopped under delta conditions.

Antonelli took the win from Max Verstappen by 4.351s, with Norris third. Lewis Hamilton retired on Lap 7 with brake failure, and almost nobody overtook anyone.

So, who are RacingNews365's Spanish GP Winners and Losers? Find out below!

Winner - Antonelli takes control

Antonelli's eighth win of the campaign was not the most emphatic of his season, but it may prove the most valuable. He qualified 0.011s off Norris and never lost touch, then took the one strategic gift the race offered.

The 20-year-old leaves Madrid on 292 points, 81 clear of team-mate George Russell and 106 ahead of Norris. Mercedes now has 503 points to Ferrari's 358.

Antonelli has not needed to take risks to build that cushion; he has simply been in position every time a race has swung, and Madrid swung his way again.

© XPBimages

Loser - Norris loses one he had won

Norris did everything asked of him and lost 15 points of value to a rule. McLaren team principal Andrea Stella conceded that some elements of racing cannot be controlled, noting the VSC came a couple of seconds too late and then ended a few seconds too early.

Norris himself argued that a rule should not decide a race, and that he was the only driver on the grid denied the cheaper stop.

At a circuit where recovery was near impossible, third was all that remained. He is 106 adrift with the season running out, which makes this the sort of afternoon a title challenge does not survive twice.

© XPBimages

Winner - Verstappen overachieves again

Second place in a Red Bull that has no business being there was voted as the drive of the weekend by F1 fans. Verstappen qualified third, 0.140s off pole, and then defended against Norris to the line.

Context matters: under the FIA's ADUO rules for 2026, Red Bull Powertrains was designated the benchmark internal combustion engine, locking the team out of the upgrade concessions handed to rivals.

Red Bull has openly disputed the methodology, saying its own data does not match the governing body's. Verstappen is sixth in the standings on 145 points, which flatters nobody except the car. Madrid was further brilliance from the 28-year-old.

© Red Bull Content Pool

Loser - Hamilton's title bid ends

Hamilton qualified fourth, within two tenths of pole, and was out of the race by Lap 7. He described the brake failure as sudden: the pedal stepping down into Turn 5, the car refusing to slow, a brush with the barrier, then the pedal going long a few corners later.

He said he did not know where it had come from, and Ferrari has not yet identified the root component.

He was reportedly told to nurse the car home rather than stop on track, protecting Leclerc's long opening stint on hards. Hamilton stays on 191 points, third, now 101 behind with the calendar shrinking.

© XPBimages

Winner - Colapinto shines again

Ninth in qualifying, seventh at the flag, and six points that move Franco Colapinto to 27 for the season.

On a track where positions barely changed hands, the Argentine kept Oscar Piastri's McLaren behind him by 1.558s and looked very competitive. Team-mate Pierre Gasly was 12th and a lap down, which sharpens the comparison considerably. Alpine sits sixth on 68 points.

Colapinto's weekend was built in qualifying, exactly as Madrid demanded, and that is the clearest evidence yet that the 23-year-old has settled into the seat.

© XPBimages

Loser - The Madring's damaging debut

The circuit's problem is structural, not circumstantial.

Drivers reported that narrow sections and badly configured corner entries left essentially nowhere to pass, with the curved braking zone into the Turn 5 chicane singled out: Oliver Bearman pointed out that braking on a curve removes the alternate line needed to go up the inside.

Verstappen went further, arguing the design should never force drivers to steer and brake at once, and offered to redo the braking zones himself. Piastri rated only Monaco harder for overtaking.

No FIA or organiser review has been confirmed, and whether anything changes before 2027 is the question Madrid now has to answer.

© XPBimages

title: Maximilian Günther signs multi-year deal in Envision Formula E switch
excerpt:
The first part of Envision's Formula E driver pairing for the start of the Gen4 era has been confirmed.

Maximilian Günther will race for Envision from the upcoming season after signing a multi-year contract, the Formula E squad has confirmed.

The seven-time race winner arrives as Envision steps up its preparations for the Gen4 era, which formally begins with pre-season testing at the Circuit del Jarama on 16-20 November.

Günther brings eight seasons of Formula E experience to the team. Born in Oberstdorf, the 29-year-old started karting at the age of 10 before moving into single-seaters in 2011.

He finished runner-up in the FIA Formula 3 European Championship in 2016 and third overall the following year, before graduating to Formula 2. His first taste of Formula E came at the 2018 rookie test in Marrakesh, which earned him a reserve role and then a race seat at GEOX Dragon for Season 5.

The breakthrough followed in his second season, when he won the 2020 Santiago E-Prix at 22 years old to become the youngest race winner in the championship's history, a record that stood until Taylor Barnard's victory in the recent season finale last month.

Günther has often shown strong pace wherever he has held a seat, although that was difficult last campaign with DS Penske. He announced his exit from the outfit following the London finale, where there were already reports of a move to Envision. If given a competitive package, the German can deliver for Envision.

"We are thrilled to announce Max as our newest driver at Paysafe Envision Formula E Team," said team principal Sylvain Filippi.

"Season 13 is going to be an important year for all teams; learning the Gen4 car as well as a new sporting format, which is going to put an even bigger focus on outright pace and speed.

"Max has proven how capable he is at delivering qualifying laps when it matters, as well as podium finishes and race wins.

"We're incredibly excited to start working with him and hit the ground running at pre-season testing in November."

Günther hails Envision's 'exceptional quality'

Günther's Formula E career has seen him race for GEOX, BMW, Nissan, Maserati and DS Penske. Representing big brands has never been an issue, of which Envision is very much one having featured in the series since the very beginning as Virgin Racing.

Envision is opting for an entirely new driver pairing for the start of Gen4, with Günther's team-mate yet to be announced. No matter who he partners, Günther could very easily prove to be a highly underrated signing.

"I'm very happy to become a Paysafe Envision Formula E driver for the Gen4 era and I really look forward to our future together," said Günther.

"The team has a very successful history in Formula E and exceptional quality throughout the organisation. Our aim is to combine our strengths and achieve great success, competing at the very top.

"I truly believe we have all the ingredients to build something really special together. What convinced me about the project was the great environment, the high ambition of the team, the mindset and, of course, the excellent technical package together with Jaguar.

"I'm proud to become part of the team and have a fantastic feeling about our future."

title: Toto Wolff reveals Kimi Antonelli anguish with 'cool' comparison
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has described Kimi Antonelli using the simile "cool as a cucumber" following his victory at the Spanish Grand Prix.

The Mercedes driver was not the quickest driver at the Madring, with that honour going to Lando Norris, but took advantage of a fortuitously timed virtual safety car to clinch his eighth win of the F1 season from second on the grid.

In doing so, the 20-year-old increased his lead over team-mate George Russell in the drivers' standings to 81 points, with eight or nine rounds to go.

However, Antonelli — and not for the first time this year — stressed out Wolff on the pit wall with his flat-out nature, despite comfortably controlling the latter stages of the 57-lap race in Madrid.

When appraising his driver's performance and his tendency to push the limit even when leading, the Mercedes team principal told Sky Sports F1: "I think he's cool - sometimes an inch too cool!

"When he brushes the wall five laps from the end and comes on the radio, 'check the car,' you're like, 'really, again, white lines, walls,' but maybe that's how he keeps himself in the zone.

"Almost his youth helps him a lot because he's 20. He could stay in this sport for 20 years with so many opportunities. He's so above all of our expectations and his own. He's just going with the flow.

"I think there is also a genetic factor. You are born cool as a cucumber, or you're not."

Wolff - 'You see junior drivers crumbling in Formula 2'

Wolff, expanding on his remarks, highlighted how Antonelli differs from other young drivers with his ability to absorb pressure without wilting from the expectations of the moment.

With a healthy advantage in the F1 drivers' championship, the Italian only needs to consistently rack up points over the remainder of the schedule.

However, he shows no signs of letting up and is perfectly content to continue in his current gear.

"You can see this in junior formula or karting - taking pressure easier," Wolff added. He's taken this to another level.

"We are talking about Formula 1. You see junior drivers crumbling in Formula 2.

"He's just doing his thing. We told him, 'This is a race where we need to bring it home, need to score points whether it's P2 or P5, we don't care, just drive it home'.

"He does that and goes fast."

title: Ferrari launch 'thorough' investigation into Lewis Hamilton brake failure
excerpt:
It's not the first time Ferrari has had brake issues with its cars this season.

Ferrari has promised a full investigation into the brake system failure that forced Lewis Hamilton out of the Spanish Grand Prix.

Hamilton had qualified fourth at the Madring, but retired after just six laps, ending his streak - and the last in F1 this season - of scoring points in every race.

The seven-time F1 champion confirmed after the race that the pedal dropped a step under braking for Turn 5, leaving him carrying too much speed and brushing a barrier. He explained that the pedal then returned to normal before going long again a few corners later.

Although Ferrari attempted to resolve the problem from the pit wall, the fault reappeared, forcing him out of the race.

"At this stage, we don't yet know the exact cause of the brake system issue that forced him to retire," said Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur, speaking to the media after the race, including RacingNews365. "But we will investigate it thoroughly.

"The pedal was long. We tried to fix it from the pit wall, and then it happened again."

A long pedal is typically traced to a hydraulic pressure loss. Ferrari has had recurring brake-feel issues this year, although it remains unclear whether the Madring failure is linked.

[Article continues below]

Long game for Leclerc

Leclerc salvaged the weekend for Ferrari with fourth, 29.116s behind race winner Kimi Antonelli and just 0.713s clear of George Russell.

The Monégasque ran an extremely long opening stint on the hard tyre as Ferrari gambled on a stoppage that never came.

"Like a few other teams, we split the strategy, starting one car on the soft compound and the other on the hard," Vasseur explained.

"With Charles, we were leading the group that started on the hard tyre, and he drove a very strong first stint, pushing for almost 50 laps while maintaining good pace throughout.

"We knew there was a reasonable chance of a safety car or a red flag, so we decided to extend the stint and keep that opportunity open.

"A red flag could have put us in a position to fight for the win, while a late safety car could have given us a shot at third. In the end neither happened, but I think it was absolutely worth trying and Charles delivered a very solid performance."

Hamilton stays third in the drivers' standings on 191 points, with Leclerc fifth on 167 heading to the next grand prix in Azerbaijan on Saturday, September 26.
